{{Please leave this line alone (sandbox heading)}} {{Infobox military conflict | conflict = Ayyubid Defense of Mayyafaraqin and Mardin | partof = Ayyubid–Georgian wars | date = c. 1209–1210 | place = Mayyafaraqin (modern Silvan) and Mardin, northern Mesopotamia (modern Turkey) | result = Ayyubid defensive victory | combatant1 = {{flagicon|Georgia (1918–1921)}} Kingdom of Georgia
Armenian allied forces | combatant2 = {{flagicon|Ayyubid dynasty}} Ayyubid Sultanate | commander1 = Ivane Mkhargrdzeli (probable) | commander2 = Al-Awhad Ayyub (probable) | strength1 = Unknown | strength2 = Unknown | casualties1 = Unknown | casualties2 = Unknown | notes = Series of defensive engagements preventing Georgian advances into northern Mesopotamia }} == Ayyubid Defense of Mayyafaraqin and Mardin (c. 1209–1210) == The **Ayyubid Defense of Mayyafaraqin and Mardin** was a series of military engagements during the Ayyubid–Georgian wars, occurring around 1209 to 1210. As the Kingdom of Georgia and its Armenian allies pushed southward into northern Mesopotamia, the Ayyubid Sultanate successfully mounted a defense of the key fortresses of Mayyafaraqin (modern Silvan) and Mardin. Under the command of Al-Awhad Ayyub, nephew of Saladin, Ayyubid forces repelled Georgian raids and counterattacks, halting the Christian advance and securing the northern frontier of the Ayyubid territories. These defensive victories played a crucial role in setting the stage for the decisive Ayyubid victory at the Siege of Ahlat in 1210. == References == * Ibn al-Athir, *Al-Kāmil fī al-tarīkh* (The Complete History), early 13th century. * Kirakos Gandzaketsi, *History of Armenia*, 13th century. * Rustamov, F., “The Georgian–Ayyubid Relations in the 12th–13th Centuries,” *Journal of Oriental Studies*, 2018. * Minorsky, V., *Studies in Caucasian History*, 1953.

{{Please leave this line alone (sandbox heading)}} {{Infobox military conflict | conflict = Counter-Raids in the Van–Vaspurakan Frontier | partof = Ayyubid–Georgian wars | date = 1208–1209 | place = Van and Vaspurakan region, Armenian Highlands (modern eastern Turkey) | result = Ayyubid tactical victory | combatant1 = {{flagicon|Georgia (1918–1921)}} Kingdom of Georgia
Armenian allied forces | combatant2 = {{flagicon|Ayyubid dynasty}} Ayyubid Sultanate and local Muslim allies | commander1 = Ivane Mkhargrdzeli (probable) | commander2 = Local Ayyubid governors (unknown) | strength1 = Unknown | strength2 = Unknown | casualties1 = Unknown | casualties2 = Unknown | notes = Series of ambushes and skirmishes repelling Georgian incursions before the Siege of Ahlat }} == Counter-Raids in the Van–Vaspurakan Frontier (1208–1209) == The **Counter-Raids in the Van–Vaspurakan Frontier** were a series of military skirmishes and ambushes conducted by Ayyubid forces and their local Muslim allies during 1208–1209. These actions took place in the Van and Vaspurakan regions of the Armenian Highlands, as Georgian and Armenian forces attempted to expand their control southwards. The Ayyubid defenders, utilizing knowledge of the terrain and local support, effectively ambushed and repelled several Georgian-led raids. These tactical victories disrupted Georgian advances and helped to prepare the defensive posture that culminated in the successful defense of Ahlat in 1210. == References == * Kirakos Gandzaketsi, *History of Armenia*, 13th century. * Vardan Areveltsi, *Universal History*, 13th century. * Ibn al-Athir, *Al-Kāmil fī al-tarīkh* (The Complete History), early 13th century. * Rustamov, F., “The Georgian–Ayyubid Relations in the 12th–13th Centuries,” *Journal of Oriental Studies*, 2018.

{{Please leave this line alone (sandbox heading)}} {{Infobox football match | title = Second-leg match of the 2018 AFF Championship final | other_titles = | image = [[File:Vietnamese people celebrate when Vietnam won the 2018 aff cup 02.jpg|245px]] | alt = | event = [[2018 AFF Championship final]] | caption = Hanoi citizens celebrate the victory on the streets after the match. | team1 = [[Vietnam national football team|Vietnam]] | team1association = {{flagicon|VIE|size=30px}} | team1score = 1 | team2 = [[Malaysia national football team|Malaysia]] | team2association = {{flagicon|MAS|size=30px}} | team2score = 0 | details = Vietnam win with aggregate 3–2 | date = {{Start date and age|2018|12|15|df=y}} | stadium = [[Mỹ Đình National Stadium]] | city = [[Hanoi]] | man_of_the_match1a = [[Nguyễn Quang Hải (footballer, born 1997)|Nguyễn Quang Hải]], [[Midfielder#Attacking midfielder|Attacking midfielder]] | man_of_the_match1atitle = [[Honor (company)|Honor]] | man_of_the_match1b = | man_of_the_match1btitle = | fair_player1 = | fair_player1title = | player_of_the_match1 = | player_of_the_match1title = | referee = [[Alireza Faghani]] ([[Football Federation Islamic Republic of Iran|Iran]]) | attendance = 44,625 | weather = Colder night
{{convert|17|C|F}}
60% [[Humidity|humidity]] | previous = | next = }} On December 15, 2018, the [[Vietnam national football team]] and [[Malaysia national football team]] played a second-leg match of the [[2018 AFF Championship final]] determine the champion of the [[ASEAN Championship|AFF Championship]] that year. Vietnam defeated Malaysia 1–0 after 90 minutes thanks to Nguyen Anh Duc's only goal in the 5th minute of the game to win with aggregate 3–2 and clinching their second championship title after their first title in [[2008 AFF Championship|2008 tournament]] over the [[Thailand national football team|Thailand]] with the same aggregate score. Previously, the two teams drew 2–2 in the first leg at the Bukit Jalil National Stadium. In this rematch, striker Nguyen Anh Duc scored the only goal in the 6th minute after an assist from Nguyen Quang Hai, giving the Vietnamese team a 1–0 victory. With a total score of 3–2 after two legs, the Vietnamese team officially won the [[ASEAN Championship]] for the second time in history, 10 years after their first victory in 2008. The match, officiated by Iranian referee [[Alireza Faghani]], was tense with a total of 11 yellow cards and 1 indirect red card (given to Shahrul Saad of Malaysia in the 90+5 minute), with the visiting team receiving 5 yellow cards and the home team receiving 6 yellow cards. In terms of media coverage, this final match set viewership ratings records in the region: In Vietnam, the average rating reached an unprecedented high of 28.14% in Hanoi and peaked at over 31%; in [[South Korea]], due to the attention given to coach [[Park Hang-seo]], [[Seoul Broadcasting System|SBS]] recorded an average rating of 18.1% and a peak of 25.3%, becoming the most-watched sports program in the country for a decade at that time. Many newspapers in Vietnam and South Korea reported on the match after Vietnam won the championship, against the backdrop of Vietnamese football achieving many impressive results in 2018. Due to the impact of the match on Vietnamese football, public opinion in this country usually only mentions the second leg whenever the final match of the tournament is discussed. == Background == {{main|2018 AFF Championship final}} [[File:Park Hang-seo 1 (cropped).JPG|270px|left|thumb|Park Hang-seo has the opportunity to win his first championship title with Vietnamese football.]] From its inaugural tournament in [[1996 AFF Championship|1996]], known as the Tiger Cup, until the 2018 edition, both the Vietnamese and Malaysian national teams were regular participants and considered strong teams in the region. The Vietnamese team participated in every edition of the tournament and won their first title in 2008 under coach [[Henrique Calisto]], after defeating [[Thailand national football team|Thailand]] in the final. Besides this title, Vietnam finished as runners-up in [[1998 AFF Championship|1998]] and consistently reached the semi-finals in 1996, [[2000 AFF Championship|2000]], 2002, [[2007 AFF Championship|2007]], [[2010 AFF Championship|2010]], [[2014 AFF Championship|2014]], and [[2016 AFF Championship|2016]]. The period from 2014 to 2016 saw consistent performance, with the team reaching the semi-finals but failing to advance to the final match. As for the Malaysian team, they also boast a similar track record, winning the championship in 2010 after defeating [[Indonesia national football team|Indonesia]] in the final.{{cite web |last= Dư|first= Hoài|date= |title= Thành tích của bóng đá Việt Nam qua các kỳ AFF Cup|url= https://tuoitre.vn/thanh-tich-cua-bong-da-viet-nam-qua-cac-ky-aff-cup-2024051815144729.htm|trans-title= Vietnam's football achievements in previous AFF Championship|website= Tuổi Trẻ|language= vi|location= |publisher= |access-date=30 April 2025}} Prior to that, Malaysia reached the first final of the tournament in 1996 but lost to Thailand. In subsequent stages, they finished as runners-up once more in 2014 and reached the semi-finals several times in 2000, 2002, [[2004 AFF Championship|2004]], and [[2012 AFF Championship|2012]]. A common characteristic of Malaysia during this period was their ability to maintain fluctuating performance but often perform effectively in knockout matches. Prior to the 2018, the history of confrontations between Vietnam and Malaysia in the AFF Championship showed a relatively balanced record, but Vietnam had a slight advantage in terms of wins. In 10 official encounters in this tournament since 1996, Vietnam won 5 matches, drew 2, and lost 3. Vietnam's biggest victory against their opponent was in the [[2002 AFF Championship|2002 tournament]] with a 2–1 score in the third-place match. However, Malaysia has held the upper hand in several crucial knockout matches. Most notably, in the 2010 semi-final, Malaysia eliminated defending champions Vietnam with a 2–0 aggregate score over two legs. In 2014, the two teams met again in the semi-final; although Vietnam won 2–1 in the first leg away from home, Malaysia won 4–2 in the second leg at My Dinh Stadium, overturning the deficit to a 5–4 aggregate score. These results have forged a long and storied rivalry between the two leading football nations in the region ahead of the 2018 final.{{cite web |last= |first= |date= |title= Lịch sử đối đầu với Malaysia nghiêng về tuyển Việt Nam|url= https://tuoitre.vn/lich-su-doi-dau-voi-malaysia-nghieng-ve-tuyen-viet-nam-20181115013607542.htm|trans-title= The head-to-head history against Malaysia favors the Vietnamese team|website= |language= vi|location= |publisher= Tuổi Trẻ|access-date=29 April 2025}} The Vietnamese national team's preparation for the 2018 AFF Championship was closely linked to a generational transition under South Korean coach Park Hang-seo. Following success at the [[2018 AFC U-23 Championship]] and the [[2018 Asian Games]], the core of the team is a combination of young players in their prime and experienced veterans. The team underwent a two-week training camp at the Paju Sports Center in South Korea in October 2018. There, Vietnam played three friendly matches against local clubs to test tactical formations such as 3–4–3 and 3–5–2. Vietnam's squad is considered to have depth, with outstanding individuals in various positions such as Đặng Văn Lâm, Quế Ngọc Hải, Nguyễn Quang Hải, and Nguyễn Anh Đức.{{cite web |last= |first= |date= 12 September 2018|title= Vietnam team to train in South Korea to prepare for AFF Championship|url= https://vietnamnews.vn/sports/465568/viet-nam-team-to-train-in-south-korea-to-prepare-for-aff-cup.html|website= vietnamnews.vn|location= |publisher= |access-date= 10 May 2026}} On the Malaysian side, the Football Association of Malaysia (FAM) appointed [[Tan Cheng Hoe]] as head coach with the goal of rebuilding their playing style.{{cite web|url=https://www.thestar.com.my/sport/football/2017/12/07/fam-tan-cheng-hoe-to-take-over-as-harimau-malaya-head-coach/|title=FAM: Tan Cheng Hoe to take over as Harimau Malaya head coach|work=The Star|date=7 December 2017|accessdate=29 June 2018}} Malaysia shifted from a physically demanding style of play to a control-oriented, short-passing style that builds attacks from their own half. To prepare for the tournament, Malaysia conducted a squad review through international friendly matches against opponents such as Sri Lanka and Kyrgyzstan. Notably, this is the first AFF Cup where Malaysia has used a naturalized player, with the case of winger [[Mohamadou Sumareh]]. The Malaysian team focused on building cohesion between veteran players and new talents from the national U-23 team, aiming to improve on their early elimination in the group stage of the tournament two years prior.{{cite web |last= |first= |date= 23 October 2018|title= Malaysia công bố 26 cầu thủ tham dự AFF Cup 2018|url= https://thethao.vtv.vn/the-thao/dt-malaysia-cong-bo-26-cai-ten-du-aff-cup-2018-20181022233110467.htm|trans-title= Malaysia announces 26-player squad for 2018 AFF Championship|website= [[Vietnam Television]]|language= vi|location= |publisher= |access-date=9 May 2026}} == Pre-match == === First-leg match === The first leg, played on December 11, 2018, at the [[Bukit Jalil National Stadium]], ended in a 2–2 draw. Vietnam took an early two-goal lead through Nguyen Huy Hung and Pham Duc Huy, but Malaysia equalized with two goals from set pieces.{{cite web |last= |first= |date= 11 December 2018|title= Malaysia, Vietnam draw in Suzuki Cup final first leg|url= https://worldsoccertalk.com/afp/malaysia-vietnam-draw-in-suzuki-cup-final-first-leg-20181211-CMS-259182.html|website= World Soccer Talk|location= |publisher= |access-date=3 January 2026}} The away-goal draw gave Vietnam a significant advantage going into the return match. According to the tournament regulations, Vietnam only needed a 0–0 or 1–1 draw in the second leg to win the championship. Conversely, Malaysia had to win or draw by a score of 3–3 or higher to secure the title in regular time.{{cite web |last= Đan|first= Hoài|date= 11 December 2018|title= Kịch bản nào để Việt Nam vô địch AFF Cup 2018?|url= https://laodong.vn/the-thao/kich-ban-nao-de-viet-nam-vo-dich-aff-cup-2018-646278.ldo|trans-title= What scenarios would lead to Vietnam winning the 2018 AFF Championship?|website= Tuổi Trẻ|language= vi|location= |publisher= |access-date=20 March 2026}} {{Football box |id = |date = {{Start date|2018|12|11|df=y}} |time = {{UTZ|20:45|8}} |event = |round = |team1 = {{fb-rt|MAS}} |score1 = 2 |team2 = {{fb|VIE}} |score2 = 2 |scorenote = |aet = |report = [http://www.aseanfootball.org/v3/wp-content/uploads/match_result/suzuki_cup/2018/M25.pdf Report (AFF)] |goals1 = [[Shahrul Saad]] {{goal|36}}

[[Muhammad Taqi (referee)|Muhammad Taqi]] ([[Football Association of Singapore|Singapore]]) |} |} === Media coverage === On December 13, 2018, [[Seoul Broadcasting System]] (SBS) announced a temporary suspension of the next episodes of the prime-time drama ''[[Fates & Furies (TV series)|Fates and Furies]]'' to dedicate the entire broadcast time to the match.{{Cite web |date=16 December 2018 |title=Park Hang-seo lauded as hero at home, in Vietnam |url=https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/www/sports/2022/12/600_260464.html |access-date=21 December 2022 |website=[[The Korea Times]] |language=en |quote=SBS, one of the nation's three major broadcasting companies, cancelled the popular TV series "Fates and Furies" to air the Suzuki Cup final.}} Previously, matches of the Vietnamese national team under the leadership of South Korean coach Park Hang-seo were mainly broadcast on the cable television channel SBS Sports.{{chú thích web|url=https://www.goal.com/kr/뉴스/박항서-매직에-동남아-월드컵-스즈키컵-사상-첫-국내-생중계/6lm9v5mvdisi10kqmzq98rn8i|title='박항서 매직'에 '동남아 월드컵' 스즈키컵, 사상 첫 국내 생중계|trans-title=SBS Sports will broadcast the main events of the 2018 AFF Championship|language=ko|publisher=Goal.com (Korea)|date=1 November 2018|access-date =9 November 2018}} However, due to increased viewer demand, the station has switched to a nationwide broadcast channel. According to media reports, the first leg match on December 11th recorded an average viewership rating of 4.706%, peaking at 7% in the second half.{{cite web |last= Jeong-hyeon|first= Lee|date= 15 December 2018|title= 완성된 박항서 매직…베트남전 실시간 시청률 16.31％|url= https://www.yna.co.kr/view/AKR20181215055000005|trans-title= Park Hang-seo's Magic Completed... Vietnam Match Live Viewership 16.31%|website= Yonhap|language= ko|location= |publisher= |access-date=30 April 2026}} === Other activities === Starting on the afternoon of December 15th, thousands of fans gathered in the square in front of [[Mỹ Đình National Stadium]]. Organized fan clubs rehearsed cheering rituals, using drums and handheld loudspeakers to coordinate the crowd. Maximum security forces were deployed to manage traffic flow and control the crowd as the vehicles carrying the two teams moved into the stadium area. In the stands, groups of fans began deploying large flags and preparing visual cheering strategies to implement as soon as the match began.{{cite web |last= |first= |date= |title= Không khí tại "chảo lửa" Mỹ Đình trước trận đại chiến Việt Nam-Malaysia|url= https://dantri.com.vn/the-thao/khong-khi-tai-chao-lua-my-dinh-truoc-tran-dai-chien-viet-nam-malaysia-2018121518165751.htm|trans-title= The atmosphere at My Dinh Stadium before the big match between Vietnam and Malaysia|website= Dân Trí|language= vi|location= |publisher= |access-date=5 May 2026}} In other major cities, public football viewing areas (Fanzones) also attracted large crowds before kick-off. In [[Hồ Chí Minh City]], the [[Nguyễn Huệ Boulevard]] area was equipped with many large LED screens, attracting tens of thousands of people gathering from around 4 PM. In other localities such as [[Đà Nẵng]], [[Hải Phòng]], and [[Cần Thơ]], many large screens were also installed in squares, cultural centers, and local stadiums to serve the needs of people who could not travel to [[Hanoi]] to watch the matches live.{{cite web |last= |first= |date= |title= Trước trận chung kết, “không nói nhiều, Việt Nam vô địch!”|url= https://dantri.com.vn/thoi-su/truoc-tran-chung-ket-khong-noi-nhieu-viet-nam-vo-dich-20181215142917883.htm|trans-title= Before the final match, "no more talking, Vietnam will be champions!"|website= Dân Trí|language= vi|location= |publisher= |access-date=5 May 2026}}
